02 / THE PROBLEM

SPACE SCIENCE IS AMAZING.
UNDERSTANDING IT CAN BE HARD.

A textbook explains thrust, heat and landing — but learners rarely see how these systems affect one another in a mission they control.

01
◈

Abstract concepts

Mass, fuel, acceleration and trajectory can feel like disconnected formulas.

02
⚠

High-stakes mistakes

Real missions cannot be repeated as a casual experiment. Students need a safe sandbox.

03
✦

Lost curiosity

Passive lessons offer fewer opportunities to explore, make choices and see consequences.

Our problem to solve: make the systems thinking behind spaceflight accessible and exciting.

03 / OUR SOLUTION

CHOOSE. BUILD. FLY. IMPROVE.

A visual game for young explorers: choose the parts you like, drag them onto a rocket, and watch the trade-offs come to life.

01 ↓
🚀

Build a rocket

Pick 5X, 10X, 15X or 20X components. Six systems: hull, engine, tank, guidance, shield, legs.

02 →
🪐

Choose a world

Start at Earth and the Moon. Open Mars and more planetary levels; choose a landing style.

03 ↗
🎮

Fly & react

Use an external route view or simulated cockpit. Manage ice, overheating and engine faults.

04 ↺
📊

Learn & retry

Read the mission report and adjust the design. Demo mode has unlimited credits and materials.

04 / SCIENCE BEHIND THE GAME

REAL IDEAS. PLAYABLE MODELS.

The game introduces rocket propellants, engine trade-offs, materials and launch conditions using NASA educational sources.

PROPULSION / 01

RP-1 + LOX

Kerosene-based fuel with liquid oxygen. The NASA Saturn V F-1 engine used this combination.

PROPULSION / 02

LH₂ + LOX

Liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. NASA RS-25 engines are associated with this high-efficiency system.

PROPULSION / 03

CH₄ + LOX

Methane and oxygen: an important current area of rocket propulsion research and development.

NASA OPEN RESOURCES

Weather + launch video

NASA POWER historical daily observations inform a simplified launch-weather risk. Real Artemis II launch footage appears as a clearly labeled reference clip.

NASA references and footage are credited. Game physics and weather risks are simplified; this is not NASA flight software or a live forecast.

06 / LEARNING OUTCOMES

THE GAME TEACHES HOW TO THINK.

Each flight becomes a small experiment. Players form a hypothesis, test it, see the result and improve their model.

THE LANDING CHALLENGE
h ≈ v² / 2a

Find when to ignite the landing engine. Change speed or braking force — and predict where the craft will land.

Educational approximation, not a real mission trajectory solver.
